tagline: Old pine-tar country, gone over to peanuts and soybeans.
intro: East of Wilson the byway picks up NC 42 and strings four state roads together across the Coastal Plain, through Pinetops, Conetoe and Hassell, 51.7 miles to Williamston on the Roanoke River. It takes about an hour.

The name comes from the pine tar trade. Fat pine was piled up, set alight and covered with soil, and the kilns were left to smolder until the resin ran out as dark tar for rope and wooden hulls. A legend credits the nickname to Cornwallis's soldiers, who came out of the Tar River with tar on their feet.

moments.title: Wilson
moments.text: Once called the world's greatest tobacco market, the city grew out of a community called Toisnot after the railroad reached it in 1839.

moments.title: Conetoe
moments.text: Founded in 1887 as Warren Station and renamed for Conetoe Creek, the little town among the soybean and peanut fields is spelled one way and said Cuh-knee-ta.

moments.title: Williamston
moments.text: Past sheds and silos full of peanuts the road reaches a Roanoke River town settled in 1779 and first called Skewarky, after the plantation it was built on.

sources.label: NCDOT, North Carolina Scenic Byways guidebook, Tar Heel Trace
